finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: The file name 'grades' is derived from an attacker-controlled source, such as a command line argument or an environment variable.
finding.assumptions: The file name 'grades' is derived from an attacker-controlled source, such as a command line argument or an environment variable.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the file name used in std::ifstream is a compile‑time constant string literal "grades" (line 15). No code path reads a filename from stdin, argv, environment, file, or any public API. No conditional or transformation of untrusted data is applied before the open, so the source cannot be attacker‑controlled.

finding.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
finding.trigger: The code does not validate or sanitize user input before using it in a dynamic memory allocation.
finding.assumptions: User input is used to determine the number of students, which is then used in a dynamic memory allocation.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the code for any untrusted data source that influences the size passed to malloc on line 26. The size argument is the literal constant 18, which is not derived from stdin, a file, network, argv, environment variables, IPC, or any caller-controlled parameter. No control flow leads from any potential user input to this allocation. Therefore the claim that untrusted input determines the allocation size is incorrect. No OS command injection path exists here.

finding.title: Buffer Over-read / Buffer Over-write
finding.trigger: The code uses 'strdup' to duplicate strings without checking the length of the input strings.
finding.assumptions: The input strings 'first' and 'last' are derived from user input and are not validated for length.

parsed.refutation_attempt: I examined the code paths from the untrusted file source to the calls on line 34 and 35. The strings `first` and `last` are read into std::string objects via `operator>>`, which ensures they are null‑terminated C strings when `c_str()` is called. `strdup` then allocates exactly `strlen(c_str())+1` bytes, so there is no fixed‑size buffer that could be overflowed. No other checks are needed to prevent an over‑read or over‑write because the allocation size matches the input length. I also verified that no other part of the code uses a fixed-size buffer that could be written past its bounds. Thus, there is no actual buffer overflow or under‑read path from the source to the sink.

finding.title: Improper Release of Memory before Returning from a Function
finding.trigger: The code does not check if 'student_ptrs[i]' is NULL before calling 'free' on it.
finding.assumptions: The code assumes that 'student_ptrs[i]' is always valid and not NULL.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the C standard regarding free(NULL) – it is defined to be a no‑op. The loop at lines 49‑54 always calls free on pointers that were allocated by malloc or strdup; if any of those allocations had failed they would be NULL, but free(NULL) is safe. Therefore the lack of explicit NULL checks does not constitute a vulnerability.
